procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order of the Gujarat High Court in Criminal Revision Application No. 145 of 1964, dated November 9, 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court allowed the Criminal Revision Application No. 145 of 1964 and set aside the conviction and sentence of Manilal Maganlal (the respondent).
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The License Inspector appealed to the Supreme Court by certificate granted by the High Court to challenge the High Court's decision to set aside the conviction. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal and maintained the order passed by the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether an erroneous interpretation of a statute, even if it has been followed for a long time since a previous High Court decision, should be upheld.

facts: The appellant's counsel argued that a specific interpretation of a statute, established by a previous Bombay High Court decision, had been followed for a long time without being contradicted by other courts.
Based on this long-standing acceptance, the appellant contended that the Supreme Court should not disturb this established view.
law: The authority to file a complaint under a statute must be explicitly granted by that statute.
An erroneous interpretation of a statute cannot confer legal authority, even if that interpretation has been followed or 'acquiesced in' for a long time.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument.
The Court distinguished this case from situations where a 'series of decisions' had established a particular view upon which various rights had been built.
It reasoned that the fundamental requirement for a person filing a complaint is to demonstrate their authority under the Act.
The Court held that this necessary legal authority cannot be created by a long-standing but incorrect interpretation of the law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that an erroneous interpretation of a statute, even if it has been followed for a long time since a single previous High Court decision, should not be upheld because a long-standing error cannot create legal authority where the statute itself does not grant it.

issue.issue_text: Whether only the authorities specified under Section 48(1) read with Section 69 of the Act are empowered to initiate proceedings for offences under the Act.

facts: A Licence Inspector filed a complaint against the respondent for an offence under the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949.
The Municipal Commissioner had delegated the power to 'take proceedings' under Section 69(1) of the Act to the Deputy Health Officer.
The Deputy Health Officer, in turn, gave permission to the Licence Inspector to file the complaint.
The respondent was convicted, but the High Court, in revision, set aside the conviction, holding that the Licence Inspector was not authorized to file the complaint.
law: The case centered on the interpretation of Section 481 read with Section 69 of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, 1949.
Section 69(1) allows the Municipal Commissioner to delegate his powers to other municipal officers.

The key legal question was the meaning of the phrase 'take proceedings' in Section 481. The High Court interpreted it to mean 'instituting a complaint' personally, not 'causing a complaint to be filed' by someone else.
application: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's interpretation.

It held that the authority to launch proceedings for offences under the Act is restricted to the specific authorities mentioned in the statute (Section 481) or those to whom power has been properly delegated (under Section 69).

The Court reasoned that the delegated power 'to take proceedings' required the authorized officer (the Deputy Health Officer) to file the complaint himself. This power did not include the ability to sub-delegate or authorize another person (the Licence Inspector) to file it.
The Court cited a similar case under the Calcutta Municipal Act, which established that only the authorities mentioned in that Act could file a complaint.

It rejected the appellant's argument that a long-standing, contrary interpretation by the Bombay High Court should be followed, stating that authority to file a complaint cannot be conferred by an 'erroneous interpretation long acquiesced in'.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that only the authorities specified in Section 481, or an officer to whom the power has been directly delegated under Section 69, can initiate proceedings. The power 'to take proceedings' does not include the power to authorize another person to file the complaint. Therefore, the complaint filed by the Licence Inspector was invalid.

issue.issue_text: Whether the phrase 'take proceedings' in the relevant statute can be interpreted to mean 'order proceedings to be taken'.

facts: A complaint was filed by a Licence Inspector.
The statutory power to "take proceedings" under s. 481 of the Act had been delegated by the Commissioner to the Deputy Health Officer.

The issue was whether the Deputy Health Officer, who was delegated the power to "take proceedings", could authorize the Licence Inspector to file the complaint, or if the Deputy Health Officer had to file it himself.
law: The relevant statute uses the phrase "take proceedings" to describe the authority to initiate legal action for offenses under the Act.
The court must interpret the plain meaning of this phrase as it is used in the English language.
application: The Court applied a plain language interpretation, stating that the word "take" is an English word and can only be given a meaning it actually bears in the English language.
It noted that no dictionary or legal authority was presented to show that the word "take" can mean "cause to be taken" or "order to be taken".

The Court explicitly rejected a practical argument that it would be an undue administrative burden for the Deputy Health Officer to have to personally sign thousands of complaints, stating, "We are not impressed by this argument."

The Court also observed that other actions listed in the same section of the Act, such as instituting a suit or compromising a claim, would undisputedly have to be performed by the delegate himself, suggesting a consistent interpretation was intended.
In doing so, the Court declined to follow a previous Bombay High Court judgment that had held "take proceedings" could mean "order proceedings to be taken".
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the phrase "take proceedings" cannot be interpreted to mean "order proceedings to be taken". The power to initiate proceedings must be exercised directly by the person to whom that power is granted or delegated. Therefore, only the delegated authority (the Deputy Health Officer) could launch the proceedings, not a subordinate acting on his orders (the Licence Inspector).

arguments.issue_text: Whether an erroneous interpretation of a statute, even if it has been followed for a long time since a previous High Court decision, should be upheld.
appellant_arguments: The decision of the Bombay High Court in The State v. Manilal Jethalal was binding on the lower court.
The view from the Manilal Jethalal case has prevailed for a long time without any other decision taking a different view, and therefore, it should not be disturbed.
respondent_arguments: The respondents were not represented before the court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether only the authorities specified under Section 48(1) read with Section 69 of the Act are empowered to initiate proceedings for offences under the Act.
appellant_arguments: The power to 'take proceedings' includes the power to authorize others to institute those proceedings.
The order delegating power to the Deputy Health Officer did not contain limiting words that he must file the complaint himself and not authorize others.
respondent_arguments: The respondents were not represented. However, the argument accepted by the High Court (and upheld by the Supreme Court) was that the complaint was filed by a Licence Inspector, who was not the person to whom the power was delegated (the Deputy Health Officer), and therefore the complaint was invalid.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the phrase 'take proceedings' in the relevant statute can be interpreted to mean 'order proceedings to be taken'.
appellant_arguments: The power to 'take proceedings' includes the power to authorize others to institute proceedings, which implies it can mean 'order proceedings to be taken'.
This interpretation was supported by the previous Bombay High Court decision in The State v. Manilal Jethalal.
respondent_arguments: The respondents were not represented. However, the argument accepted by the High Court (and upheld by the Supreme Court) was that the expression 'take proceedings' means instituting a complaint personally and does not mean causing a complaint to be filed by someone else.

cases.case_name: T. P. Thakur v. Ratilal Motilal Patel
cases.principle: A person who files a complaint under an Act must show that he has the authority to file that complaint, and that authority cannot be conferred upon him by an erroneous interpretation long acquiesced in.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Only the authorities specified within the governing Act have the legal standing to initiate proceedings for offenses under that Act, its rules, regulations, or bye-laws. A complainant must demonstrate this specific authority, which cannot be established merely through a long-standing but erroneous interpretation of the law.
obiter: The principle of stare decisis does not protect a single, erroneous interpretation of a statute where no significant rights have accrued to parties acting on that view.
The meaning of the words 'take proceedings' is to be ascribed the meaning it bears in the English language and cannot be interpreted to mean 'order proceedings to be taken'.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The authority to initiate legal proceedings for offences under the Act is strictly limited to the officials explicitly named in the statute. The phrase 'take proceedings' requires the designated authority to personally launch the action, and does not include the power to delegate the filing of the complaint to a subordinate. An erroneous interpretation of a statute, even if it has been followed for a long time based on a single prior court decision, cannot confer legal authority where none exists.
legal_tests_applied: Strict Statutory Interpretation: A person who files a complaint under the Act must show that he has the authority to file that complaint, and that authority must be derived directly from the statute.

Stare Decisis Limitation: The principle of not disturbing a long-prevailing judicial view does not apply to a single, erroneous interpretation of a statute, especially when it is not a case where a series of decisions have been widely accepted and various rights have accrued to parties acting on that view.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that a long-standing but erroneous High Court decision should be upheld, stating, 'A person who tiles a complaint under the Act must show that he has the au1hori1y 10 file that complaint and that authoriy cannot be conferred upon him by an erroneous intcrrre:aiion Jon~ acquiesced in.'

The court determined that the conditions for applying the doctrine of stare decisis were not met, noting, 'This is not a case where a series of decisions have taken a particular view and that view has been widely accepted and various right• have accrued :o parties acting on that view.'

The court did not accept the broad interpretation that the power to 'take proceedings' includes the power to authorize others to file the complaint, thereby affirming that the complaint was filed by an unauthorized person.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed the principle that only the specific authorities mentioned in the statute could launch proceedings against persons charged with offences under the Act.
The complaint was fundamentally invalid because the person who filed it lacked the statutory authority to do so, as this power had not been, and could not be, delegated to them.
policy_considerations: The court upheld the rule of law principle that the authority to prosecute must be clearly and explicitly granted by statute, and cannot be created by judicial interpretation or long-standing practice.

The court's reasoning implies a preference for legislative clarity, noting that if the legislature intended to allow for delegation of complaint-filing, 'it would have been perfectly easy to use 1he words which find place in several Acts, for example, "except upon a complaint in writing of the Commissioner or an officer to whom he has delegated his powers."'.
